title: Clock and Ledger
premise: In 1911 London, Astrid Delacroix drives for the suffragist Miriam Halloway and quietly reads every letter that passes through her hands, certain that history is a thing that happens to other people. When a census taker's probing questions about the household's unregistered boarders — a runaway seamstress, a deserter cousin, and a child no one will claim — draw the attention of an inspector with a ledger of his own, Astrid is pulled into a conspiracy of sheltered lives. As the household fractures under surveillance and Miriam faces arrest, Astrid must secure passage to Canada for those she has come to love, ending with the wrenching dawn choice of which family member takes the last berth aboard the morning-tide ship — and her discovery that belonging is not given but chosen, at cost.
about_author: Silas Ravensworth is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing suffrage-era letters in a Yorkshire county records office before turning to fiction. He writes in a converted tollhouse, where he keeps a 1911 census form framed above his desk as a reminder that every name was once a person.

chapters.title: The Driver's Hands
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. We meet her at dawn, polishing the motorcar and memorizing the day's letters before Miriam Halloway sees them — a habit born of an orphanage childhood where information was survival. Astrid insists history happens elsewhere. Emotional beat: guarded competence masking loneliness.

chapters.title: A Census of Small Deceptions
chapters.summary: The census taker, Mr. Pell, arrives on census night and asks one question too many about the extra faces in the house: seamstress Odette, deserter cousin Tomas, and the mute child Wren. Astrid lies smoothly; Pell writes something down anyway. POV: Astrid. Beat: the first crack — being noticed.

chapters.title: Letters I Shouldn't Have Read
chapters.summary: Astrid reads a letter warning Miriam that her name is on an inspector's list. She nearly burns it, instead hides it. POV: Astrid, with a flashback to the orphanage ledger where her own name was once crossed out. Beat: fear that history has found her address.

chapters.title: The Household of Borrowed Names
chapters.summary: Miriam's POV. We see the house as she built it: a refuge of aliases and second suppers. She knows Astrid reads the letters and says nothing, testing loyalty. Beat: two women circling each other, both keeping secrets out of care.

chapters.title: Inspector Vane's Ledger
chapters.summary: Inspector Vane, POV his, arrives with Pell's notes and a ledger of 'irregular persons.' He interviews Astrid, who gives nothing but notices he carries a photograph of his own lost daughter. Beat: the antagonist revealed as wounded, dangerous, human.

chapters.title: Wren Speaks in Chalk
chapters.summary: The child Wren, who cannot or will not speak, draws chalk warnings on the pavement — a man watching the house. Astrid realizes the child understands more than anyone. POV: Astrid. Beat: tenderness; the found-family bond takes root.

chapters.title: Rally at Caxton Hall
chapters.summary: Astrid drives Miriam to a suffrage rally; police violence erupts and Astrid, against all instinct, wades in to pull Odette from a constable's grip. Her name is taken. Beat: history stops happening to other people; she is inside it now.

chapters.title: The Deserter's Confession
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV his, tells Astrid why he deserted — a firing squad refused, a brother lost — and asks if the house can hold him much longer. Astrid promises it can, a promise she may not keep. Beat: the weight of other people's survival on her shoulders.

chapters.title: Passage and Price
chapters.summary: Astrid visits the shipping office about emigration to Canada and learns berths cost more than the household can raise — and that Vane has asked the line to flag departures. Beat: the escape plan is born under a tightening noose.

chapters.title: Miriam's Arrest
chapters.summary: Miriam is taken at a peaceful deputation, choosing arrest deliberately as testimony. Astrid watches the door close and understands she is now the household's spine. Beat: grief and terrible promotion — from driver to guardian.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: POV Odette. The house without Miriam: rationed coal, whispered plans, Wren's night terrors. Odette and Astrid clash over whether to run now or hold the house as Miriam would. Beat: found family fracturing under fear.

chapters.title: Vane's Offer
chapters.summary: Vane corners Astrid: give up the deserter and the child's irregular status disappears; his daughter's photograph trembles in his hand. Astrid refuses, and understands she has made an enemy with a personal wound. Beat: moral stakes sharpened.

chapters.title: What the Letters Said
chapters.summary: Astrid confesses to the household that she has read their letters for years — and that this is how she found the shipping agent's loophole. Betrayal and gratitude collide. Beat: honesty as the price of true belonging.

chapters.title: Night of the Raids
chapters.summary: Police raid the street. Tomas hides in the coal cellar; Astrid stalls Vane at the door with a forged census page, using his own paperwork against him. Beat: the climax's engine starts; no going back.

chapters.title: The Forged Berth
chapters.summary: Astrid forges a fourth name on the passage list — her own — then learns the ship allows only three berths before the manifest seals at dawn. Beat: the book's central dilemma made concrete and ticking.

chapters.title: Miriam's Letter from Holloway
chapters.summary: A letter from prison, smuggled out: Miriam releases Astrid from obedience — 'Choose as a mother chooses, not as a servant.' Astrid reads it aloud to the household. Beat: blessing and burden; the choice is truly hers.

chapters.title: Tomas Decides
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV his, surrenders quietly at a recruiting office to buy the others time, asking Astrid to tell Wren he was brave. Beat: sacrifice reframes the berth question — but a berth remains unclaimed by choice, not resolution.

chapters.title: Vane at the Dock Gate
chapters.summary: Vane intercepts Astrid at the docks, ledger in hand, and sees Wren's chalk drawing in her bag — his daughter once drew the same stars. He hesitates. Beat: the antagonist's crisis; the climax hangs on a held breath.

chapters.title: The Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Climax. On the gangway, the final berth must go to one of three: Odette, Wren, or Astrid herself. Astrid puts Wren in Odette's arms, gives the steward the forged name, and steps back onto the dock as the ship casts off. Beat: the choice made at cost; history witnessed from the shore.

chapters.title: What the Inspector Wrote
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. He closes his ledger with a single line: 'No irregular persons at this address.' He mails Astrid the photograph of his daughter. Beat: mercy as the antagonist's redemption; the hunt ends not in victory but in recognition.

chapters.title: The House That Kept Its Names
chapters.summary: Astrid, Miriam freed on appeal, and the emptied house. They repaint Wren's chalk stars on the front step so she can find her way back from across the sea. Beat: mourning transformed into belonging; the family persists beyond walls.

chapters.title: Letters, Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Epilogue, a year on: Astrid now reads letters aloud at the kitchen table, no longer stealing them. A letter arrives from Odette and Wren in Canada; the last line is in a child's handwriting. Beat: memory, found family, and the quiet triumph of being someone history happened to — and who happened back.
